He and other senior officers moved toward the danger as reports emerged from multiple locations across the city. Karkare’s death was mourned nationally and came to symbolize the risks faced by police and security personnel confronting the attackers.

At hospitals and morgues, relatives searched for missing loved ones while officials struggled to identify victims and notify families. Some people waited through the night for news; others learned that relatives who had been traveling, working or sharing a meal had been killed. Foreign governments sought information about their citizens, while communities in India and abroad organized memorials and offered assistance to survivors.

The personal accounts emerging from Mumbai revealed the indiscriminate nature of the violence. The dead included children and parents, workers and travelers, police officers and bystanders, Indians and foreign nationals. Beyond the statistics, each loss represented a family altered permanently and a community forced to grieve. # Lives cut short in Mumbai: Remembering the victims behind the headlines

**MUMBAI, India —** The November 2008 terrorist attacks unfolded across India’s financial capital in a cascade of gunfire, explosions and fire, targeting hotels, a railway station, a Jewish center and other crowded locations.

Over nearly three days, 10 gunmen carried out coordinated assaults that killed 166 people and wounded hundreds more. Behind that toll were families, public servants, travelers and religious leaders whose lives converged in Mumbai.

Among them were an American father and daughter on a spiritual journey, a senior police officer who headed toward danger, and a young Jewish couple who had built a welcoming home far from where they grew up.

## Alan and Naomi Scherr: A father and daughter traveling together

Alan Scherr, 58, and his daughter Naomi, 13, had traveled from Virginia to India with members of the Synchronicity Foundation, a meditation community.

They were eating at the Oberoi-Trident hotel when gunmen attacked.

Alan Scherr was remembered as a devoted father and longtime meditation teacher. Naomi, his only child, was described by those who knew her as bright, compassionate and unusually poised for her age.

Their deaths resonated deeply in their Virginia community, where friends recalled the close bond between father and daughter. They had come to India seeking reflection and fellowship, only to become two of the Americans killed in the siege.

## Hemant Karkare: The police chief who answered the call

Hemant Karkare, 54, was the head of Maharashtra state’s Anti-Terrorism Squad.

As reports of attacks spread on the night of November 26, Karkare put on protective gear and joined the police response. He was killed near Cama Hospital alongside senior officers Ashok Kamte and Vijay Salaskar when attackers opened fire on their vehicle.

Karkare’s career had placed him at the center of some of India’s most sensitive terrorism investigations. Colleagues described him as methodical, disciplined and committed to following evidence despite political pressure.

His death came to symbolize the risks taken by Mumbai’s police officers, many of whom confronted heavily armed assailants with limited equipment and little information about the scale of the operation.

## Rabbi Gavriel and Rivka Holtzberg: A home open to strangers

Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg, 29, and his wife, Rivka, 28, ran the Chabad center at Nariman House, also known as Mumbai’s Jewish House.

The couple had moved to Mumbai to serve the city’s small Jewish community and Jewish travelers passing through India. Their center offered religious services, kosher meals and a place to stay. Visitors remembered the Holtzbergs for welcoming strangers as if they were family.

Gunmen seized Nariman House and held people inside during a prolonged standoff. Indian commandos later stormed the building, but the Holtzbergs and several others were found dead.

Their 2-year-old son, Moshe, survived. He was carried from the building by his nanny, Sandra Samuel, who had hidden with him before escaping. Images of the frightened child in her arms became among the most enduring scenes of the attacks.

The couple’s deaths were mourned around the world. In Mumbai, the Chabad center was later reopened, continuing the mission of hospitality they had begun.

## Remembering people, not numbers

The Mumbai attacks struck some of the city’s most recognizable landmarks, including the Taj Mahal Palace hotel, the Oberoi-Trident complex and Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus. But their impact extended far beyond those buildings.

The victims included hotel employees who helped guests escape, railway passengers on their way home, police officers and commandos, businesspeople, tourists, children and members of several faiths and nationalities.

Alan and Naomi Scherr, Hemant Karkare, and Gavriel and Rivka Holtzberg came from different countries and lived very different lives. Their stories remain part of the human legacy of an attack remembered not only for its scale, but for the individual futures it erased.

**166 Killed in Mumbai Attacks, Leaving Families and Communities in Mourning**

**MUMBAI, India —** The coordinated terrorist attacks that paralyzed Mumbai for nearly three days have left 166 victims dead and more than 300 people injured, devastating families across India and around the world.

The dead included commuters, hotel guests and employees, police officers, railway workers, diners and members of Mumbai’s Jewish community. Indians made up most of those killed, but victims also came from the United States, Britain, Israel and several other countries.

Gunmen struck sites woven into the city’s daily life and identity: the crowded Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus railway station, the Taj Mahal Palace and Oberoi-Trident hotels, the Leopold Cafe and the Jewish center at Nariman House. What began as an evening of ordinary journeys, meals and work shifts became a prolonged siege marked by gunfire, fires and desperate searches for missing relatives.

At hospitals and temporary help centers, families waited for names to be posted and called mobile phones that went unanswered. Some learned that relatives had escaped; others were asked to identify bodies. Survivors faced injuries and trauma, while many families confronted the sudden loss of primary earners, parents, children and spouses.

Among the dead were senior police officials Hemant Karkare, Ashok Kamte and Vijay Salaskar, killed while responding to the attacks. Railway police officer Tukaram Omble was also killed while helping capture the sole surviving attacker. Hotel employees died while trying to guide guests to safety, becoming symbols of courage amid the violence.

At Nariman House, six people were killed, including Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg and his wife, Rivka. Their young son survived after being carried from the building by his nanny, an image that came to embody both the attacks’ cruelty and the bravery of those who tried to save others.

The toll extends beyond those killed and wounded. Thousands of witnesses, emergency workers and residents endured days of uncertainty. Businesses closed, neighborhoods fell silent and religious communities began funeral rites for victims whose lives had intersected only briefly in the places the attackers chose.

Across Mumbai, vigils and memorials are bringing together people of different faiths and nationalities. Candles, flowers and handwritten messages have appeared outside the railway station, hotels and cafes.

As the city begins to reopen, the scale of the loss is becoming clearer one family at a time: an empty place at a dinner table, a missed train home, a hotel worker who did not return from a shift. Behind the casualty figures are 166 lives and communities now facing the long work of grief and recovery.

**Mumbai’s Dead Included Police Commanders, Hotel Workers, Travelers and a Young Jewish Family**  
*By Staff Correspondent*  

**MUMBAI, Dec. 1, 2008** — As India began burying the dead from last week’s coordinated assault on Mumbai, the names emerging from hospitals, hotels, police stations and foreign consulates gave a human dimension to an attack initially measured in explosions, gunfire and burning buildings.

The three-day siege, which began on the evening of Nov. 26, killed 166 victims and wounded hundreds. The dead included senior Indian police officers, commandos, hotel employees, commuters, business travelers, religious workers and tourists from several countries. Nine of the 10 gunmen were also killed; the sole surviving attacker was taken into custody.

Among the most prominent Indian casualties was **Hemant Karkare**, 54, the chief of the Maharashtra Anti-Terrorism Squad. Karkare put on a helmet and bulletproof vest and went into the streets soon after reports of shootings at the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus and other locations.

He was killed near Cama Hospital alongside **Ashok Kamte**, an additional commissioner of police, and **Vijay Salaskar**, a veteran police inspector known for pursuing organized-crime figures. The three officers were traveling together when gunmen opened fire on their vehicle. Their deaths, early in the attack, deprived the police response of several of its most experienced commanders.

Karkare had recently become a controversial public figure while overseeing an investigation into a bombing in the predominantly Muslim town of Malegaon. His funeral drew senior officials and large crowds, and his death was mourned across India as that of an officer killed while confronting the Mumbai attackers.

Kamte, remembered by colleagues as physically imposing and calm under pressure, had gone toward the fighting despite having responsibility for another part of the city. Salaskar had spent years in Mumbai’s crime branch and was widely identified in the Indian press as an “encounter specialist,” a term used for officers involved in armed confrontations with suspected gangsters.

Two members of India’s security forces were also among the best-known dead.

**Maj. Sandeep Unnikrishnan**, 31, of the National Security Guard, was killed during operations at the Taj Mahal Palace and Tower hotel. According to accounts released after the battle, he was leading commandos through the hotel when a colleague was wounded. Unnikrishnan continued in pursuit of the gunmen and was fatally shot. His death prompted public tributes in his native Kerala and at his family home in Bangalore.

At Nariman House, the Jewish center also known as Chabad House, **Havildar Gajender Singh**, a commando from the NSG’s 51 Special Action Group, was killed during the attempt to retake the building. Commandos descended by helicopter onto the roof before fighting their way through the structure.

Inside Nariman House, rescuers found the bodies of **Rabbi Gavriel Holtzberg**, 29, and his wife, **Rivka Holtzberg**, 28. The couple, emissaries of the Chabad-Lubavitch movement, had made the center a place of worship and hospitality for Jewish visitors to Mumbai.

Their 2-year-old son, Moshe, survived after being carried from the building by his Indian nanny, **Sandra Samuel**, who found him near his mother during the siege. Images of the crying child in Samuel’s arms became among the most wrenching of the attack. The Holtzbergs were later buried in Israel.

Other victims at the Jewish center included **Rabbi Aryeh Leibish Teitelbaum**, an American-born religious supervisor who lived in Jerusalem, and **Bentzion Chroman**, a dual American-Israeli citizen. The center’s dead reflected its role as a destination for religious visitors as well as the apparently deliberate targeting of a Jewish institution.

At the Oberoi-Trident hotel complex, two Americans from Virginia, **Alan Scherr**, 58, and his daughter **Naomi Scherr**, 13, were killed. They had traveled to India with members of the Synchronicity Foundation, a meditation community based in Virginia. Friends described father and daughter as deeply devoted to one another. Naomi was among the youngest foreign victims identified in the first days after the attack.

Also killed at the Oberoi was **Lo Hwei Yen**, 28, a Singaporean lawyer traveling on business. She was reported to be Singapore’s first citizen killed in a terrorist attack. Her death was confirmed after an anxious wait by her family and colleagues as security forces searched the hotel.

Among the British dead was **Andreas Liveras**, 73, a Cyprus-born shipping and luxury-yacht businessman. Liveras had been dining at the Taj hotel and spoke by telephone to the British Broadcasting Corporation while trapped during the attack. He described gunfire and confusion before contact was lost. His death was later confirmed.

The Taj’s casualties included members of the family of **Karambir Kang**, the hotel’s general manager. Kang remained at work helping coordinate the evacuation while fire swept through parts of the building. His wife, **Neeti**, and their two sons, **Uday** and **Samar**, died after becoming trapped in their room. Their deaths came to symbolize the sacrifices made by hotel employees, many of whom stayed behind to guide guests through service corridors and away from the attackers.

Numerous hotel workers were killed while assisting guests, though many of their names initially received less international attention. Employees at both the Taj and Oberoi were credited by survivors with locking doors, leading groups to stairwells and kitchens, and returning repeatedly to areas still under fire.

The largest single scene of killing was not one of the luxury hotels but **Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus**, Mumbai’s crowded railway station. Gunmen armed with assault rifles and grenades fired into commuters and railway employees. Many victims there were ordinary residents traveling home from work, and some remained unidentified for days or were known publicly only through lists posted at hospitals and police stations.

Others died at the **Leopold Café**, a popular restaurant frequented by Indians and foreigners; near **Cama Hospital**; in a taxi explosion; and during attacks around south Mumbai.

The casualty lists reflected Mumbai itself: wealthy travelers and low-paid workers, Indians and foreigners, Hindus, Muslims, Jews and Christians. Citizens from the United States, Israel, Singapore, Britain, Germany, Italy, Canada, Australia, Japan and other countries were reported among the dead.

In the days after the siege, funerals took place under heavy security, hotel employees gathered for memorials, and relatives moved between morgues and hospitals seeking confirmation. Photographs of the dead appeared in newspapers beside accounts of last telephone calls and unsuccessful attempts to escape.

The attacks had been aimed at prominent symbols — a railway terminus, landmark hotels and a Jewish center — but the victims were not symbols. They were police officers who drove toward gunfire, commandos entering darkened buildings, workers who stayed to help guests, parents traveling with children, and commuters caught in one of the world’s busiest stations.
